title: Scarcity and economising
context: Analyze scarcity, economising, and who participates in economic decision-making. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Scarcity disappears once a household earns a steady salary because income removes all limits.
Economising means making careful use of limited resources rather than treating them as if they were unlimited.
Nobody can fully opt out of economic decisions, because even inaction is a choice about scarce time or money.
Only registered businesses face scarcity; households with regular income never need to economise on their spending.
Exchange requires that at least one party is an entrepreneur; households can never participate directly in exchange.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — Even steady income is finite and must be allocated among competing needs and wants.
TRUE — Economising is the rational response to scarcity: using limited resources as efficiently as possible.
TRUE — Choosing not to spend or not to act still allocates a scarce resource and therefore counts as an economic decision.
FALSE — Households also face limited budgets and must economise; scarcity is not confined to businesses.
FALSE — Households routinely exchange money or goods for products and services; they are active trading partners.

title: Goods, services, needs, and wants
context: Analyze the distinction between goods, services, needs, and wants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Goods must be intangible; any tangible item automatically counts as a service instead.
Services are intangible activities performed for someone, such as installing software or preparing a drink.
Needs are things necessary for well-being, whereas wants are desired but not essential for basic well-being.
Both households and businesses have needs that may be fulfilled through exchange with other economic actors.
Scarcity means resources are limited, so individuals and businesses must economise rather than assume unlimited supply.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — Tangible physical items are goods; intangibility defines services, not the reverse.
TRUE — Services are activities performed for a customer rather than physical objects taken away.
TRUE — Needs concern necessity for well-being; wants are preferences that go beyond what is strictly necessary.
TRUE — Entrepreneurs and firms have operational needs just as households do, such as supplies and labour.
TRUE — Limited resources force economising behaviour on both households and businesses facing scarcity.

title: Households, entrepreneurs, and everyday exchange
context: Analyze the roles of households and entrepreneurs in everyday exchange of goods and services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Only consumers ever exchange goods; businesses are legally barred from all trade with households.
Only individual consumers have needs; registered businesses operate with zero internal needs of their own.
Choosing to keep pocket money unspent means a teenager has avoided making any economic decision.
Exchange is one way needs and wants get fulfilled when households and businesses trade with each other.
Because money is used, barter arrangements can never count as genuine exchange.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — Businesses and households routinely trade goods and services with each other in markets.
FALSE — Businesses and entrepreneurs also have operational needs, such as raw materials and a workforce, not only consumers.
FALSE — Saving or holding cash is itself a choice about how to use a scarce resource.
TRUE — Exchange is precisely how needs and wants on both sides of a transaction can be fulfilled.
FALSE — Exchange includes barter where no money changes hands; monetary payment is not required for a trade to count.

title: Business Operations and Institutional Needs
context: Consider households, startups, and manufacturing firms interacting in a market system. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Businesses provide goods like computers and services like installing software for people to satisfy their needs.
Manufacturers of smartphones may have an operational need for electronic components produced by specialised suppliers.
To fabricate components, a manufacturer requires raw materials and a workforce rather than operating in isolation.
Individuals frequently exchange goods and services directly and are fully active participants in trading.
Households need food, shelter, and medical care, and they also want leisure activities such as cinema visits.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Firms supply tangible goods and intangible services that help consumers satisfy needs.
TRUE — Component manufacturers depend on specialised inputs to assemble finished devices.
TRUE — Production requires limited inputs and labour; no firm can operate without securing those resources.
TRUE — Individuals trade with businesses and with each other; households are not excluded from exchange.
TRUE — Household demand spans essential needs and non-essential wants such as entertainment.

title: Corner café: beans and cappuccinos
context: Consider a corner café where customers buy bags of coffee beans and pay baristas to prepare drinks. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bag of roasted beans is a good and the barista's drink preparation is a service.
Needs and wants are identical concepts, so there is no meaningful difference between craving caffeine and a flavoured latte.
A habitual craving for a particular drink is more accurately a want if it is not essential for basic well-being.
Because the café is a business, it cannot itself be said to have needs such as reliable suppliers.
Paying for beans or drinks fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides of the transaction.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Beans are tangible goods; preparing and serving a drink is a service performed for the customer.
FALSE — Needs concern necessity for well-being; wants are desired but not essential, so the concepts differ.
TRUE — A preferred drink beyond basic nutrition is typically classified as a want rather than a strict need.
FALSE — Businesses have operational needs including suppliers, staff, and premises to stay open.
TRUE — Monetary payment for goods or services is exchange that satisfies needs or wants.

title: Jonas: bus pass or game skin
context: Consider jonas has twelve euros pocket money and must choose between an eight-euro bus pass and a ten-euro game skin. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bus pass is a need for getting to school, while the game skin is a want rather than a basic necessity.
Because both items have a price, they must both be classified as needs rather than wants.
Individuals face economic decisions about scarce resources even before they run a business or register as entrepreneurs.
Choosing to save the twelve euros and buy nothing means Jonas has opted out of all economic decision-making.
Once Jonas buys the bus pass, his want for the game skin permanently disappears and can never return.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Needs are necessary for well-being; getting to school is a need, while a game skin is a desired but non-essential want.
FALSE — Having a price does not make something a need; the distinction rests on necessity for well-being, not on cost.
FALSE — Individuals with pocket money already participate in the economy and face choices about limited resources.
FALSE — Saving or doing nothing is itself an economic decision about how to use a scarce resource.
FALSE — Satisfying one need does not erase a want; Jonas may still want the skin even after buying the pass.

title: PhoneFix screen repairs
context: Consider phoneFix Wien replaces cracked screens using spare parts ordered in limited monthly batches. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Screen replacement is a service, while a phone case sold at the counter is a good.
Because PhoneFix is a business rather than a household, its monthly spare parts can never run scarce.
A customer buying a decorative case purely for its design is satisfying a want rather than a basic need.
Repairing a phone never fulfils a need because phones are luxury items outside normal economic analysis.
A limited monthly batch of parts forces the shop to economise by prioritising which jobs to accept.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Repair work is an activity performed on the device (service); a case is a tangible product (good).
FALSE — A fixed monthly batch is by definition limited and therefore scarce.
TRUE — Buying for design enjoyment rather than necessity reflects a want, not a strict need.
FALSE — A working phone for daily communication can represent a genuine household need.
TRUE — Scarce spare parts require prioritisation and careful allocation among repair jobs.

title: Defining the economy from scratch
context: Consider during a first lesson students list core building blocks of economic life. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The economy consists essentially of households and entrepreneurs interacting with one another.
Goods are tangible items, whereas services are intangible activities performed for someone.
Both households and businesses have needs, and exchange is one way those needs and wants get fulfilled.
Scarcity forces individuals and businesses to economise rather than assume unlimited resources.
Nobody, whether a household or a business, can truly opt out of making economic decisions.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Households and entrepreneurs are the two foundational groups in the basic economic picture.
TRUE — Tangible versus intangible is the core distinction between goods and services.
TRUE — Needs and wants on both sides motivate exchange between households and firms.
TRUE — Limited resources relative to wants make economising necessary for all actors.
TRUE — Even choosing inaction allocates scarce resources and therefore remains an economic decision.

title: Herr Novak's bakery
context: Consider herr Novak sells bread at his Linz bakery and charges one euro extra for doorstep delivery. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Herr Novak acts as an entrepreneur, while the families buying his bread act as households.
Bread is a good and doorstep delivery is a service, matching the distinction between tangible and intangible offerings.
Because Herr Novak owns a business, he personally has no needs of his own.
Paying for delivery is not exchange because a service has no monetary value once it has been performed.
Flour and oven fuel are unlimited for any bakery, so Herr Novak never has to economise on ingredients.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — A shop owner supplying products is an entrepreneur; customers purchasing them are households.
TRUE — Bread is tangible and therefore a good; delivery is an activity performed and therefore a service.
FALSE — Entrepreneurs have needs too, such as reliable suppliers, staff, and premises to keep operating.
FALSE — Paying money for a service is a standard form of exchange, just like paying for a good.
FALSE — Ingredients and fuel are limited, purchasable resources that any bakery must economise on.

title: Exchange without money
context: Assess statements about exchange, barter, and fulfilling needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Two neighbours swapping gardening lessons for a handmade bookshelf still counts as exchange even without money.
Exchange can only occur when euro banknotes or electronic transfers are used between the parties.
Wood used to build the bookshelf is a limited resource, so the carpenter must economise on how much he uses.
Gardening lessons are a service because they are an activity performed for the neighbour, not a physical item.
Individuals, not only businesses, have needs and wants that direct exchange can help satisfy.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Barter still fulfils needs or wants on both sides and therefore qualifies as exchange.
FALSE — Exchange is not limited to monetary transactions; barter is a recognised form of trade.
TRUE — Raw materials like wood are scarce and require careful allocation across projects.
TRUE — Lessons are intangible activities performed for someone and are classified as services.
TRUE — Households and individuals participate in exchange and hold needs and wants like firms do.

title: Petra's dining table commission
context: Consider petra pays carpenter Fabian 650 euros for an oak dining table he builds and delivers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Petra's family acts as a household and Fabian acts as an entrepreneur in this transaction.
The finished dining table is a good because it is a tangible item Fabian produces and delivers.
Paying for the table fulfils the family's need for furniture through exchange.
Fabian has no genuine need for timber because raw materials are merely wants for any business.
Timber is a limited resource, so Fabian must economise on how much oak he uses per commission.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — A family buying a custom product is a household; a self-employed craftsperson is an entrepreneur.
TRUE — A physical table handed over to the buyer is a tangible good.
TRUE — Money paid for the table is exchange that fulfils the household's need for usable furniture.
FALSE — Businesses have real needs for inputs such as timber to continue operating and fulfilling orders.
TRUE — Timber supply is limited and costly, requiring economising on material use.

title: Needs, wants, and who has them
context: Analyze claims about needs, wants, and which actors in the economy face them. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A manufacturer of laptops may need specialised electronic components from suppliers to keep production running.
High-tech manufacturers have zero internal needs because only end consumers ever experience genuine need.
Households buy goods and services from businesses to satisfy both needs and wants in daily life.
Wants disappear automatically once every need has been fully satisfied in a given month.
Teenagers with pocket money are outside the economy until they register a business or join a formal household.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Firms have operational needs for inputs such as components and materials to manufacture products.
FALSE — Businesses have genuine operational needs for inputs, labour, and customers, not only final consumers.
TRUE — Households routinely purchase goods and services from firms to meet needs and wants.
FALSE — Wants can persist even after needs are met; satisfying one does not erase the other category.
FALSE — Individuals participate economically through consumption and choice long before becoming entrepreneurs.

title: Lukas end-of-month pocket money
context: Consider student Lukas has 300 euros monthly for transport, toiletries, and designer trainers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Ninety euros for transport and toiletries covers needs, while 140-euro trainers cover a want.
Because Lukas receives money from parents, he is not part of the household side of the economy.
Buying trainers makes his need for transport disappear for the rest of the month.
Wanting trainers is irrational and therefore falls outside the scope of economics entirely.
A fixed monthly sum is an unlimited resource that never needs to be economised.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Transport and toiletries are necessary; designer trainers are desired but not essential.
FALSE — Receiving parental support does not exclude Lukas from household consumption decisions.
FALSE — One purchase does not eliminate ongoing needs such as transport for the month.
FALSE — Economics studies wants as well as needs; non-essential desires are within its scope.
FALSE — A capped monthly allowance remains limited and requires allocation choices.

title: Farmer Reinisch's market stall
context: Consider farmer Reinisch sells potatoes and carrots from eight hectares at a Saturday village market. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Reinisch acts as an entrepreneur at the stall while village buyers act as households.
Because farmland can theoretically be bought elsewhere, Reinisch's eight hectares should not be treated as scarce.
Potatoes and carrots are goods rather than services even though they must be cooked before eating.
Splitting eight hectares between crops is an economic decision Reinisch cannot avoid given limited land.
Paying cash at the stall is not genuine exchange because only barter counts as real economic trade.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — A producer selling at market is an entrepreneur; purchasing families are households.
FALSE — Reinisch's actual eight hectares remain fixed and scarce for his planting decisions regardless of land elsewhere.
TRUE — Vegetables are tangible items and therefore goods, regardless of preparation before consumption.
TRUE — Fixed acreage forces allocation between competing crop uses.
FALSE — Cash payment for produce is a standard monetary form of exchange.

title: Market day in Hallstatt
context: Consider toni sells cheese wheels; Rosa offers children's face-painting; families buy for groceries or fun. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Toni and Rosa act as entrepreneurs while visiting families act as households.
A cheese wheel is a good and face-painting is a service.
Buying cheese for weekly groceries satisfies a need, while face-painting satisfies more of a want.
Paying for cheese or face-painting fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides.
Because Toni has only thirty wheels left, he must economise by allocating stock among queuing families.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Stallholders supply goods or services; buyers are households purchasing them.
TRUE — Cheese is tangible; face-painting is an activity performed on the customer.
TRUE — Weekly food is a need; optional entertainment is a want.
TRUE — Monetary payment for goods or services is exchange fulfilling needs or wants.
TRUE — A fixed remaining stock is a scarce resource requiring careful allocation.

title: Scarcity across actors
context: Assess whether scarcity and economising apply uniformly. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A multinational corporation with large cash reserves still faces scarce managerial attention and factory capacity.
Households never economise because their wants are unlimited and budgets therefore do not constrain them.
Governments are excluded from scarcity because they can always raise taxes to fund any project immediately.
Economising is rational behaviour when a resource is limited relative to competing uses.
Entrepreneurs must economise on inputs such as labour hours and raw materials to stay viable.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Even cash-rich firms face limited time, capacity, and attention among competing projects.
FALSE — Household budgets are finite and force trade-offs between competing wants and needs.
FALSE — Governments face budget limits within a given period and must allocate among projects.
TRUE — Economising responds directly to scarcity by prioritising among alternative uses.
TRUE — Firms allocate limited inputs across production, hiring, and investment choices.

title: Kaffee Ecke morning queue
context: Consider owner Sami sells bean bags and employs baristas; a rare Ethiopian lot is limited to forty kilograms. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Sami supplies goods and services as an entrepreneur while customers act as households.
The bean bag is a good and espresso preparation is a service.
A strong habitual coffee craving may reflect a want rather than a strict survival need.
Trying a new seasonal flavour for enjoyment is best classified as a want.
The forty-kilogram cap forces Sami to economise on how he allocates beans across the season.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — A shop owner providing products and drinks is an entrepreneur; buyers are households.
TRUE — Beans are tangible goods; drink preparation is a service.
TRUE — Habitual preference beyond basic nutrition typically qualifies as a want.
TRUE — Seasonal flavour trials for pleasure are wants, not necessities.
TRUE — A fixed bean batch is scarce and requires seasonal allocation decisions.

title: Classmates swap novels for algebra help
context: Consider nora lends Felix novels; Felix tutors her two afternoons with no money exchanged. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Exchange requires money, so this novels-for-tutoring swap does not count as exchange at all.
Felix's tutoring is a service and Nora's novels are goods, matching the standard classification.
Because both are students rather than businesses, needs, wants, and exchange concepts do not apply.
Felix's limited free time is a scarce resource allocated between tutoring and his other commitments.
Once the swap is agreed, both have opted out of any further economic decisions about their time.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — Exchange includes barter; money is not a prerequisite for a trade that fulfils needs or wants.
TRUE — Novels are tangible items (goods); tutoring is an activity performed (service).
FALSE — Economic concepts apply to individuals and students, not only to registered firms.
TRUE — Time is limited and must be allocated among competing uses.
FALSE — Agreeing to one swap does not end ongoing choices about remaining time and resources.

title: Opting out of the economy?
context: Analyze whether households or businesses can successfully opt out of economic decisions. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Retired couples growing their own food still face scarcity of land, time, and seed and must economise.
Repairing a customer's bicycle at a workshop is a service because it is work performed rather than an item handed over.
Selling surplus eggs to neighbours for cash is exchange that fulfils buyers' needs or wants.
Because retirees no longer earn wages, they must be classified as entrepreneurs rather than households.
Deciding how much land to plant versus how many chickens to keep is an unavoidable economic choice.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Even subsistence living involves limited land, time, and inputs that must be allocated carefully.
TRUE — Activities performed for a customer are services even when physical parts are attached.
TRUE — Trading eggs for money is exchange even on a small scale between neighbours.
FALSE — Retirement status does not turn a household into an entrepreneur; role depends on the activity, not age.
TRUE — Splitting limited land and animals between competing uses is a classic scarce-resource decision.

title: Remote cabin and firewood trade
context: Consider karl lives in a remote cabin and occasionally trades firewood for canned food from hikers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The occasional firewood-for-food trade is exchange fulfilling needs even without shops nearby.
Because Karl avoids shops, he has genuinely opted out of making economic decisions.
Karl's claim that he needs nobody proves scarcity no longer applies to him personally.
Chopping firewood requires no economising because forests are unlimited resources for anyone living remotely.
Only members of registered businesses or official households are affected by needs, wants, and scarcity.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Barter with hikers still fulfils needs through direct exchange.
FALSE — Remote living still involves choices about firewood, food, and time.
FALSE — Scarcity of labour, food, and firewood still applies regardless of social isolation.
FALSE — Accessible firewood and labour effort remain limited and require allocation.
FALSE — Economic concepts apply to individuals generally, not only formally registered units.

title: Electrician Boris and the Hoffmanns
context: Consider the Hoffmanns pay Boris 180 euros for kitchen wiring; that evening Boris buys groceries for his family. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The Hoffmanns act as a household paying for repair; Boris acts as an entrepreneur supplying it.
Electrical repair is a service because it is work performed rather than a physical item delivered.
Faulty wiring created a need for a working system fulfilled through exchange of money for service.
When Boris buys groceries later, he acts as a household with needs of his own.
Boris's limited working hours are a scarce resource he must economise across jobs.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — A family purchasing repair is a household; a tradesperson supplying it is an entrepreneur.
TRUE — Repair work is an activity performed on the property and is a service.
TRUE — A functioning electrical system is a need met by paying for professional repair.
TRUE — The same person can be entrepreneur in one transaction and household in another.
TRUE — Limited hours force prioritisation among competing repair jobs.

title: Goods versus services traps
context: Review subtle classification traps distinguishing goods from services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Installing software on a customer's computer is a service, not a good, even though it involves a physical machine.
A downloadable e-book file is a service because it has no weight and therefore cannot be a good.
Only goods, never services, can be exchanged in a market between households and firms.
A restaurant meal eaten on the premises is a good because food is always tangible.
Delivery of a pizza to a customer's door converts the pizza from a service into a good.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Software installation is an activity performed for the customer and is classified as a service.
FALSE — Digital products can still be goods when they are transferable items, even without physical weight.
FALSE — Services such as repairs, haircuts, and transport are routinely exchanged for payment.
FALSE — A prepared meal served and consumed on site is typically the service of catering, not merely a good.
FALSE — Delivery is a service added to a good; classification of the pizza itself does not flip categories.

title: Street musician tips
context: Consider elena busks on the main square; listeners drop coins into her case for violin performances. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Elena's performance is a service because it is an activity enjoyed rather than a physical item handed over.
Listeners paying because they enjoy the atmosphere are satisfying a want rather than a basic survival need.
Because each tip amount is voluntary and unfixed, no exchange takes place between Elena and the listeners.
Elena's need to cover rent shows that individuals, not only registered businesses, experience economic needs.
Elena's limited performing time each Sunday is a scarce resource she must economise across locations.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Live music is an intangible activity supplied to listeners and classified as a service.
TRUE — Enjoying atmosphere is not essential to survival and therefore reflects a want.
FALSE — Voluntary payment still constitutes exchange when money is given in return for the performance.
TRUE — Individuals face needs such as housing costs regardless of whether they operate a formal company.
TRUE — Limited hours force a choice about where and when to perform for the best return.

title: Hair salon: cut versus shampoo
context: Consider sabine pays twenty-five euros for a haircut and may buy a shampoo bottle at the counter. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The haircut is a service and the shampoo bottle is a good.
Because Sabine pays for both with money, both must be classified as goods rather than services.
Timo the self-employed hairdresser has no needs of his own since he is on the entrepreneur side.
Sabine's regular six-week visits mean scarcity no longer applies because the purchase became routine.
Paying for either item still involves exchange that can fulfil a need or want.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — An activity performed on a person is a service; a bottle taken home is a good.
FALSE — Payment method does not determine classification; a paid haircut remains a service.
FALSE — Entrepreneurs have personal and business needs despite their role as suppliers.
FALSE — Routine repetition does not eliminate scarcity of time and money on each decision.
TRUE — Monetary payment for a good or service is exchange fulfilling needs or wants.

title: Exchange breadth
context: Analyze how broadly exchange can occur between households and businesses. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Households exchange with firms when they buy groceries, and with other households when they sell used furniture.
Only entrepreneurs are entitled to exchange; households may consume but never trade.
Barter between two individuals still counts as exchange when each gives something the other values.
Exchange always requires a written contract registered with a government authority to be valid.
Paying with a mobile app transfer is exchange just like paying with coins or banknotes.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Households trade with businesses and can trade with each other in second-hand markets.
FALSE — Households are active traders when they purchase, sell, or barter goods and services.
TRUE — Non-monetary swaps that fulfil needs or wants qualify as exchange.
FALSE — Everyday purchases do not require formal contracts to constitute exchange.
TRUE — Electronic payment is a monetary form of exchange like cash.

title: Soup kitchen volunteers
context: Consider volunteers cook free soup using donated vegetables and a church kitchen lent at no charge. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Because soup is free, no recipient need is fulfilled and no exchange occurs in any sense.
Donated vegetables, kitchen time, and volunteer labour are limited and require economising.
Absence of money means volunteers and recipients have fully opted out of economic decisions.
Choosing which vegetables to use first is an unavoidable economic decision given limited supplies.
The church lending its kitchen has no needs of its own because it is not a for-profit business.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — Free provision can still fulfil recipients' need for food even without a price tag.
TRUE — Donated inputs and volunteer time remain scarce relative to how many people could be fed.
FALSE — Lack of money does not remove choices about allocating limited resources.
TRUE — Portion sizes and ingredient order reflect scarce-resource allocation decisions.
FALSE — Non-profit organisations still have needs, such as getting their kitchen back for other uses.

title: Needs of businesses
context: Review whether businesses themselves have operational needs in addition to household needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A smartphone assembler needs specialised electronic components from suppliers to manufacture devices.
Businesses have zero internal needs because only final consumers experience genuine need.
An entrepreneur needs customers and revenue to keep staff employed and operations running.
Operational needs of firms include workforce, premises, and raw materials, not only consumer demand.
If a firm is profitable, scarcity no longer applies to any of its inputs.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Production relies on component inputs that firms genuinely need to assemble finished products.
FALSE — Firms have operational needs for inputs, labour, and sales, not only end consumers.
TRUE — Without customers and revenue, a business cannot sustain employment and operations.
TRUE — Firms require physical and human inputs as needs distinct from household consumption needs.
FALSE — Profitability does not make inputs unlimited; capacity and materials remain scarce.

title: Cannot opt out
context: Analyze the claim that nobody can fully opt out of making economic decisions. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Choosing to hoard cash under a mattress is still an economic decision about using a scarce resource.
Only people who run businesses make economic decisions; pure consumers never face scarcity.
Doing nothing with a weekly allowance is opting out of economics because no purchase occurred.
Retirees living on a pension no longer make economic decisions because income is guaranteed.
Children too young to earn wages are entirely outside economic life and never economise.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Saving or hoarding allocates scarce money and is an economic choice.
FALSE — Consumers constantly decide how to spend limited income and time.
FALSE — Not spending is itself a decision about resource allocation.
FALSE — Pensioners still choose how to allocate fixed income among competing uses.
FALSE — Children with limited toys, time, or pocket money already face scarcity and choices.

title: Household wants beyond basics
context: Assess the range of household needs and wants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Households need food, shelter, and medical care to maintain basic well-being.
Sports, cinema visits, and café outings are examples of wants rather than strict needs.
A household buying cinema tickets is satisfying a want through exchange with a business.
Households and entrepreneurs interact when families purchase goods and services from firms.
Limited household income forces economising between essential needs and discretionary wants.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Basic nutrition, housing, and healthcare are core examples of household needs.
TRUE — Leisure and dining out are desired but not essential and are classified as wants.
TRUE — Paying for entertainment is monetary exchange fulfilling a want.
TRUE — Purchases from firms are the standard household–entrepreneur interaction.
TRUE — Finite income requires prioritising among needs and wants.

title: Cerny family September budget
context: Consider the Cerny family has 1,400 euros after rent for groceries, school supplies, and an optional weekend trip. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Groceries and school supplies are needs, while the weekend trip is a want.
The fixed 1,400-euro remainder is a limited resource the household must economise.
School supplies bought for children count as needs of the household as a whole.
Deciding whether to book the trip is an economic decision because inaction is also a choice.
If the family skips the trip, their want for it is permanently erased and can never return.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Essentials for living and schooling are needs; a leisure trip is a non-essential want.
TRUE — A fixed budget is scarce relative to everything the family might like to fund.
TRUE — The household is the relevant unit; supplies for children are household needs.
TRUE — Postponing or rejecting the trip still allocates the scarce budget and counts as a decision.
FALSE — An unmet want may persist; skipping this month does not erase future desire for the trip.

title: Households and Entrepreneurs in Exchange
context: Analyze how households and entrepreneurs interact when goods and services change hands. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A family selling a used bicycle online remains a household even while acting as a seller.
Exchange requires identical needs on both sides before any trade can occur.
Only multinational corporations count as entrepreneurs under basic economic definitions.
Households supply finished goods to entrepreneurs while firms supply only unpaid advice.
Repair workshops are households because customers visit the premises in person.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Households can sell possessions; role depends on the transaction, not permanent classification.
FALSE — Different needs and wants on each side motivate exchange between actors.
FALSE — Sole traders and small shops are entrepreneurs when they sell output.
FALSE — Households typically buy from firms; firms supply goods and services to households.
FALSE — The business supplying the repair is the entrepreneur; buyers are households.

title: Mira's Market Lunch Choice
context: Consider Mira, who has fifteen euros for either a hot lunch or saving toward winter boots. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Mira's fifteen euros are a limited resource she must allocate between lunch today and future boot savings.
Once Mira buys lunch, scarcity disappears for the rest of the school term.
Choosing to save rather than eat out still counts as an economic decision about scarce money.
The hot lunch satisfies a need for nutrition while designer boots would reflect more of a want.
Only business owners participate in the economy; students with pocket money are excluded.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Fixed pocket money creates scarcity requiring a choice between competing uses.
TRUE — One meal does not remove ongoing limits on money and competing wants.
TRUE — Saving allocates the limited budget and therefore remains an economic choice.
TRUE — Food supports well-being as a need; fashion boots are typically classified as a want.
FALSE — Household consumption and saving are core economic participation.

title: Goods Versus Services Distinctions
context: Review how economists classify tangible goods and intangible services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A restaurant meal consumed on the premises combines goods with the service of preparation and serving.
Installing a heat pump in a home is a service even though the pump itself is a capital good.
Legal advice becomes a good once the lawyer writes a fee invoice.
Digital delivery automatically converts every product into a tangible good.
Textbooks are services because knowledge inside them is intangible.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Catering involves service activity even when food ingredients are tangible.
TRUE — Installation work performed on site is classified as a service activity.
FALSE — Billing does not change classification; advice remains a performed service.

TRUE — High price generates excess supply relative to quantity demanded.
TRUE — Price adjustment is a coordination mechanism toward equilibrium.

title: Linz Rental Housing Listings
context: Consider Linz landlords listing flats who cut asking rents when units sit vacant for several weeks. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: At equilibrium rent, the number of vacant units neither grows nor shrinks persistently across weeks.
New apartment construction shifting supply rightward can lower equilibrium rent if demand stays fixed.
Cutting asking rent reduces quantity demanded because tenants prefer costlier apartments.
Vacant flats persisting for weeks prove asking rent is below equilibrium because tenants avoid cheap flats.
Heavy tenant competition always lowers equilibrium rent because landlords fear regulation.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Balanced market clears listings without ongoing surplus or shortage.
TRUE — Increased supply at each price can reduce equilibrium price.
FALSE — Lower rents generally increase quantity demanded for rental housing.
FALSE — Long vacancies typically signal price above equilibrium, not below it.
FALSE — Strong demand typically supports higher equilibrium rents unless supply expands.

title: Surplus in Product Markets
context: Analyze conditions where quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a given price. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A surplus exists when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the prevailing price.
Surplus puts downward pressure on price because sellers compete to reduce excess stock.
Price above equilibrium is consistent with shortage because buyers crave expensive goods.
Rapid sell-outs and empty shelves typically signal a surplus at the current price.
A harvest bumper crop eliminates surplus because larger supply always matches demand exactly.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Surplus means sellers offer more than buyers purchase at that price.
TRUE — Competition among sellers with unsold goods tends to lower price.
FALSE — High price tends to reduce quantity demanded and can leave unsold supply.
FALSE — Empty shelves signal shortage; surplus appears as unsold stock.
FALSE — Larger supply at fixed price can create surplus unless demand shifts too.

title: Shortage in Product Markets
context: Review conditions where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Long queues and rapid sell-outs often signal a shortage at the posted price.
A price ceiling set below equilibrium can create persistent shortage in a competitive market.
At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied until price adjusts.
Shortage puts upward pressure on price as buyers compete for limited available units.
A shortage exists when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the prevailing price.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Excess demand at a price appears as queues and quick stock depletion.
TRUE — Legally capped low prices can leave quantity demanded above quantity supplied.
TRUE — Low price generates excess demand relative to quantity supplied.
TRUE — Competition among buyers for scarce goods tends to raise price.
FALSE — That description defines surplus; shortage is excess demand.

title: Salzburg Festival Ticket Queue
context: Consider Salzburg festival-goers queuing overnight when discounted early-bird tickets sell out within minutes. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Minutes-long sell-outs at the posted price suggest quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
Overnight queues form when buyers expect shortage at the official price.
Persistent shortage forces resellers to cut prices below the sold-out official rate.
Adding extra performances shifts demand leftward because audiences dislike additional shows.
Raising the official ticket price increases shortage because fewer buyers withdraw.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Quick sell-outs indicate shortage at the ticket price.
TRUE — Queues signal excess demand relative to tickets available at that price.
FALSE — Scarcity at low official prices often supports higher resale prices.
FALSE — Extra performances increase supply, not reduce buyer demand directly.
FALSE — Higher prices generally reduce quantity demanded, easing shortage pressure.

title: Income as a Demand Shifter
context: Analyze how changes in consumer income shift demand for normal and inferior goods. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Income changes shift the entire demand curve rather than moving along it.
For inferior goods, rising income can shift demand leftward as buyers switch to higher-quality substitutes.
A recession reducing household income shifts demand rightward for discretionary electronics.
Higher consumer income shifts demand leftward for normal goods because buyers save everything.
A pay rise for office workers lowers equilibrium coffee price because richer buyers demand discounts.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Non-price income effects shift demand; own-price changes move along the curve.
TRUE — Higher income may reduce demand for some lower-quality goods.
FALSE — Lower income typically reduces demand for discretionary purchases.
FALSE — Normal goods see higher demand when income rises.
FALSE — Stronger demand with fixed supply typically raises equilibrium price.

title: Tastes and Preferences
context: Review how changing consumer tastes and preferences shift the demand curve. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Advertising that increases brand preference shifts demand rightward for the advertised good.
Seasonal fashion trends shifting tastes can change equilibrium clothing prices within a year.
A health trend favouring oat milk can shift demand rightward for oat beverages at each price.
When substitutes become fashionable, demand for the original good may shift leftward.
Negative publicity about a product shifts supply leftward because producers feel discouraged.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Stronger preference raises quantity demanded at each price.
TRUE — Demand shifts from taste changes alter equilibrium when supply responds.
TRUE — Preference changes shift demand independently of own-price movements.
TRUE — Changing preferences toward substitutes reduce demand for the original.
FALSE — Publicity affects buyer willingness; it is a demand shifter, not a supply shifter.

title: Styrian Wine Tasting Boom
context: Consider a Styrian wine route that sees surging visitor numbers after international tasting awards. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Surging visitor demand with limited tour slots can create shortage at the posted tasting price.
Award publicity can shift demand rightward for regional wine tastings at unchanged ticket prices.
Higher equilibrium tasting fees may result if demand shifts right while supply remains constrained.
Raising tasting fees can reduce shortage by lowering quantity demanded along the demand curve.
Expanded visiting hours shift demand leftward because tourists dislike longer schedules.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Excess demand at a fixed price produces shortage.
TRUE — Improved tastes and awareness shift demand at each price.
TRUE — Rightward demand shift with limited supply raises equilibrium price.
TRUE — Higher own-price reduces quantity demanded and can ease excess demand.
FALSE — More tour capacity shifts supply; schedule length alone does not shift demand.

title: Prices of Substitute Goods
context: Analyze how the price of substitute goods shifts demand for a related product. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Firms monitor substitute pricing because cross-price shifts alter their equilibrium sales.
Substitute price changes shift demand rather than causing movement along the demand curve.
Cheaper streaming subscriptions may shift demand leftward for cinema tickets.
Coffee shops see lower demand when nearby tea prices increase because beverages are complements.
A rise in petrol prices shifts demand leftward for public transport because travel becomes undesirable.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Substitute prices affect demand and therefore market outcomes.
TRUE — Cross-price effects shift demand; own-price changes move along the curve.
TRUE — Lower substitute prices reduce demand for the original good at each price.
FALSE — Tea and coffee are substitutes; costlier tea can boost coffee demand.
FALSE — Higher petrol cost often raises demand for substitute transport options.

title: Prices of Complementary Goods
context: Review how the price of complementary goods shifts demand for a related product. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A rise in game console prices may shift demand leftward for compatible game titles.
When complements become costlier, equilibrium quantity of the paired good may fall.
Reduced air fares can shift demand rightward for airport parking and hotel rooms near terminals.
Lower printer prices can shift demand rightward for ink cartridges.
Complementary price changes shift demand for the related good, not supply directly.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Costlier complements reduce demand for the paired good at each price.
TRUE — Higher complement prices shift demand left and can lower equilibrium quantity.
TRUE — Cheaper travel boosts demand for complementary services.
TRUE — Cheaper complements raise demand for the paired good at each price.
TRUE — Cross-price complement effects operate through demand shifts.

title: Electric Bus Fleet Procurement
context: Consider a municipal transport office comparing electric bus bids after diesel fuel costs spike. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Higher diesel costs can shift demand rightward for electric buses as substitutes become costlier.
A subsidy lowering effective purchase price shifts demand rightward for electric buses.
Expanded battery production shifting supply rightward can reduce equilibrium electric bus prices.
If electric bus prices stay fixed while demand shifts right, surplus appears at current contract offers.
At equilibrium contract price, manufacturers deliver buses cities refuse to operate.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Costlier diesel vehicles raise demand for electric alternatives.
TRUE — Lower effective buyer price increases quantity demanded at each market price.
TRUE — Greater supply at each price lowers equilibrium when demand is unchanged.
FALSE — Rightward demand at fixed price tends toward shortage, not surplus.
FALSE — Equilibrium coordinates plans; refused deliveries imply imbalance, not equilibrium.

title: Input Costs and Supply
context: Analyze how changes in production costs shift the supply curve. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: When energy costs surge, equilibrium price may rise if demand remains unchanged.
Higher wages paid to warehouse staff can shift supply leftward for distribution services.
Cheaper imported components can shift supply rightward and lower equilibrium price.
Input cost changes move producers along the supply curve without shifting it.
A drop in steel prices shifts demand leftward because buyers expect weaker furniture.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Leftward supply shift with fixed demand raises equilibrium price.
TRUE — Rising input costs reduce quantity supplied at each price.
TRUE — Lower costs increase supply and can reduce equilibrium price.
FALSE — Production costs are supply shifters that shift the curve.
FALSE — Cheaper inputs shift supply; buyer expectations are a separate demand factor.

title: Technology and Productivity
context: Review how technological improvements shift supply by lowering production costs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Technological progress that cuts unit cost shifts supply rightward, not leftward.
Improved irrigation technology may shift supply rightward for orchard fruit at each market price.
Automated sorting equipment can shift supply rightward for parcel delivery services.
Technology changes are supply shifters distinct from movements caused by the good's own price.
Rightward supply shifts from technology raise equilibrium price when demand is unchanged.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Lower costs per unit increase quantity supplied at each price.
TRUE — Productivity gains increase quantity supplied at given prices.
TRUE — Technology lowering costs increases quantity supplied at each price.
TRUE — Productivity affects supply curve position; own-price moves along it.
FALSE — More supply at unchanged demand tends to lower equilibrium price.

title: Plant Capacity Expansion
context: Consider a manufacturing plant adding a production line that raises monthly output without raising unit prices. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: If demand stays fixed while supply shifts right, equilibrium price may fall.
At the new equilibrium, quantity traded may exceed the old equilibrium if demand is unchanged.
Higher raw-material input prices could partially offset the expansion by shifting supply leftward.
Customers ordering the product face lower shortage risk after a successful supply expansion.
Adding capacity that lowers unit cost can shift supply rightward for the manufactured good.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Greater supply with unchanged demand lowers equilibrium price.
TRUE — Rightward supply shift with fixed demand raises equilibrium quantity.
TRUE — Rising material costs reduce quantity supplied at each price.
TRUE — Increased quantity supplied reduces excess demand at prior prices.
TRUE — Expanded efficient capacity increases quantity supplied at each price.

title: Number of Sellers in a Market
context: Analyze how entry or exit of sellers shifts market supply. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: New bakeries opening on the same street shift supply rightward for local bread.
Exit of several suppliers during a crisis can create shortage at previously stable prices.
Entry of low-cost online retailers can lower equilibrium prices for standardised goods.
Farmers exiting a crop after poor seasons shift supply leftward for that harvest.
Market supply equals the largest individual seller's supply ignoring smaller rivals.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — More sellers increase market quantity supplied at each price.
TRUE — Leftward supply shift can leave quantity demanded above quantity supplied.
TRUE — Rightward supply shift with stable demand reduces equilibrium price.
TRUE — Fewer sellers reduce market quantity supplied at each price.
FALSE — Market supply aggregates all sellers, not only the dominant firm.

title: Producer Expectations and Supply
context: Review how sellers' expectations about future prices influence current supply decisions. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: If producers expect costs to fall next month, some may delay production, shifting current supply leftward.
Expected future shortages motivate producers to halt current output entirely.
Expectations of higher future wheat prices increase current supply as farmers dump inventory.
Expectations about future conditions move producers along today's supply curve only.
Storage decisions based on future price outlook leave current market supply unchanged.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Expected future cost declines can reduce current quantity supplied.
FALSE — Expectations of future scarcity can encourage greater current production.
FALSE — Expecting higher future prices can encourage holding stock back from current market.
FALSE — Expectations shift supply; own-price changes move along the curve.
FALSE — Stored goods are not currently supplied; storage affects available supply.

title: Harvest Season Labour Contracts
context: Consider Styrian vineyards signing seasonal picker contracts before grape sugar levels peak. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Expectations of a large harvest can shift supply rightward for contract picker labour in August.
Timely contract signing before peak harvest can reduce later shortage when sugar levels spike.
If offered wages sit below equilibrium, vineyards may face shortage of available pickers.
Competing fruit regions raising wages may shift supply leftward for pickers in Styria.
Higher offered day rates typically increase the quantity of pickers willing to supply labour.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Anticipated output needs increase quantity of labour supplied at each wage.
TRUE — Early secured supply eases imbalance when demand for pickers surges.
TRUE — Below-equilibrium wage leaves quantity demanded above quantity supplied.
TRUE — Higher wages elsewhere reduce quantity supplied locally at each wage.
TRUE — Higher own-price of labour raises quantity supplied along the supply curve.

title: Simultaneous Demand and Supply Shifts
context: Analyze how concurrent shifts in demand and supply affect equilibrium price and quantity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The net effect on equilibrium price depends on the relative size of demand and supply shifts.
Graphical analysis compares new intersection points to identify changed equilibrium outcomes.
If demand shifts right while supply shifts left, equilibrium price is likely to rise.
If demand shifts right and supply shifts right together, equilibrium quantity rises.
Supply and demand shifts can occur together after a natural disaster disrupts production and tastes.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Ambiguous price outcomes require comparing shift magnitudes.
TRUE — New curve positions determine updated equilibrium price and quantity.
TRUE — Stronger demand with reduced supply pushes price upward.
TRUE — Both shifts increase equilibrium quantity though price change is ambiguous.
TRUE — Real events can move both curves in the same period.

title: Price Ceilings Below Equilibrium
context: Review how a legal maximum price set below equilibrium creates shortage in competitive markets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Non-price rationing such as queues may appear when ceilings create persistent shortage.
A ceiling set above equilibrium is not binding because market price stays below the cap.
Rent controls set below market equilibrium can leave landlords with fewer units to lease.
At the ceiling price, quantity supplied typically exceeds quantity demanded.
A price ceiling below equilibrium prevents price from falling to eliminate surplus.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Scarce goods at capped prices may be allocated by waiting.
TRUE — Non-binding caps do not constrain market-clearing prices.
TRUE — Shortage may reduce maintenance incentives though quantity demanded exceeds supplied.
FALSE — Binding ceilings create shortage, not surplus.
FALSE — Below-equilibrium caps block price rises that would reduce shortage.

title: Graz Rent-Control Apartment Search
context: Consider Graz tenants searching legacy rent-controlled flats while open-market leases advertise higher monthly rates. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Long waiting lists for controlled units signal excess demand at the regulated rent.
Controlled rents below open-market levels can create persistent shortage of available flats.
Landlords may redirect maintenance spending when regulated rents cover rising costs poorly.
Tenants ignore non-price costs when money rents stay capped because flats are abundant.
Open-market leases advertising higher rates prove equilibrium rent lies below the controlled cap.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Queues indicate quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at that price.
TRUE — Binding low rents leave quantity demanded above quantity supplied.
TRUE — Low regulated returns can affect supply quality and availability over time.
FALSE — Scarcity at capped rents often imposes search and waiting costs.
FALSE — Higher unregulated rents indicate the cap sits below market equilibrium.

title: Price Floors Above Equilibrium
context: Analyze how a legal minimum price set above equilibrium creates surplus in competitive markets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A price floor above equilibrium prevents price from falling to eliminate surplus.
Government purchase programs sometimes accompany agricultural price floors to absorb surplus.
At the floor price, quantity supplied typically exceeds quantity demanded.
A floor set below equilibrium is not binding because market price stays above the minimum.
Minimum prices intended to help sellers eliminate all unsold stock immediately.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Legal minimums block downward adjustment that would clear excess supply.
TRUE — Official buying can offset excess supply created by high minimum prices.
TRUE — Binding high minimums leave excess supply relative to quantity demanded.
TRUE — Non-binding floors do not constrain market-clearing prices.
FALSE — Floors above equilibrium can produce unsold surplus despite seller protection intent.

title: Minimum Wage in Labour Markets
context: Review how a wage floor above equilibrium can create surplus labour supplied. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Labour markets use wages as prices coordinating workers' supply and employers' demand.
Employers reduce quantity demanded of labour when mandatory wages rise above equilibrium.
A minimum wage set below equilibrium is not binding for market outcomes.
A minimum wage above the market-clearing wage eliminates all unemployment immediately.
At a binding minimum wage, every worker willing to work finds employment instantly.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Wage adjustment balances quantity supplied and demanded of labour.
TRUE — Higher mandated wages reduce hiring along the labour demand curve.
TRUE — Non-binding wage floors do not alter market-clearing employment.
FALSE — Binding floors can produce surplus labour, often appearing as unemployment.
FALSE — Shortage of jobs relative to willing workers reflects labour surplus at the floor.

title: Alpine Dairy Milk Quota Meeting
context: Consider an Alpine dairy cooperative setting a seasonal milk quota after feed costs jump and output surges. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Higher feed costs can shift supply leftward for raw milk at each farmgate price.
Cutting quota levels after a glut can help move the market toward equilibrium by reducing surplus.
If farmgate price stays fixed while feed costs rise, farmers expand output to celebrate.
A cooperative quota limiting deliveries increases quantity supplied by forcing extra production.
Surging milk output without matching demand creates shortage at the old farmgate price.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Rising input costs reduce quantity supplied at each price.
TRUE — Restricting supply eases excess supply at unchanged prices.
FALSE — Higher costs at fixed price typically reduce profitable supply.
FALSE — Quotas restrict supply rather than expand it.
FALSE — Output surges at fixed demand tend toward surplus, not shortage.

title: Inflation as Rising Price Levels
context: Analyze inflation as a sustained increase in the overall price level across an economy. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Inflation is measured using price indices that track many goods and services together.

Households purchasing the same basket notice inflation when that basket costs more over time.
Moderate inflation reduces the real purchasing power of money held without interest.
Inflation describes a one-day sale discount on a single retail product.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Broad indices capture general price level changes.
TRUE — Policy makers respond to inflation trends with monetary tools.
TRUE — Rising cost of a typical basket signals higher general prices.
TRUE — Higher price levels buy fewer goods per currency unit.
FALSE — Single-product price cuts are not economy-wide inflation.

title: Too Much Money Chasing Goods
context: Review the explanation that inflation can result when too much money pursues available goods and services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Inflation from monetary expansion differs from a single crop failure raising one food price.
If everyone spends newly printed money quickly, aggregate demand can rise faster than supply.
Inflation may accelerate when money supply growth outpaces growth in real output.
Holding other factors fixed, larger money supply reduces spending pressure on limited goods.
Too much money chasing too few goods explains deflation in monetary economics.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — General inflation differs from isolated relative price spikes.
TRUE — Spending surges can bid up prices when supply responds slowly.
TRUE — Excess money relative to goods tends to raise general prices.
FALSE — Greater money supply typically increases nominal spending pressure.
FALSE — That phrase describes inflationary pressure, not deflation.

title: Central Bank Note-Issuance Debate
context: Consider policymakers debating faster note issuance to fund bridge repairs while shopkeepers report rising supplier invoices. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Shopkeepers reporting broadly rising supplier invoices suggest upward pressure on the price level.
Inflation erodes the real value of cash savings when prices rise faster than interest earned.
Funding repairs through new money may increase spending before additional goods and services appear.
Rapid note issuance without matching output growth can contribute to inflationary pressure.
Policymakers weighing note issuance must consider whether output can absorb extra spending.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Widespread input price rises can feed general inflation.
TRUE — Higher price levels reduce what saved money buys.
TRUE — Spending can rise ahead of supply when money supply expands.
TRUE — Excess money growth relative to goods can raise general prices.
TRUE — Supply capacity matters when evaluating inflation risk from monetary expansion.

title: Interest Rates and Inflation Control
context: Analyze how raising interest rates can be used to reduce inflationary pressure. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Higher interest rates can reduce borrowing and spending, easing inflationary demand pressure.
Higher rates reward saving and can shift spending from today to later periods.

Monetary tightening through higher rates aims to align money growth with sustainable output.
Central banks may raise policy rates when inflation persistently exceeds target.

TRUE — Increased return on saving reduces current consumption demand.
TRUE — Costlier loans reduce quantity demanded for credit-sensitive purchases.
TRUE — Policy seeks to prevent excess money from outpacing real production.
TRUE — Tighter monetary policy responds to sustained price level increases.

title: Tightening Monetary Policy
context: Review how central banks tighten policy by raising interest rates to combat inflation. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Higher mortgage rates following policy tightening can reduce quantity demanded for new housing loans.
Central banks face a trade-off timing challenge because rate effects appear with lags.
Tightening monetary policy typically involves raising key interest rates or reducing money growth.
Business investment accelerates when higher rates raise the cost of financed equipment purchases.
Policy tightening can never reduce inflation because spending is fixed.

TRUE — Monetary policy influences inflation gradually, not instantly.
TRUE — Tighter policy restricts monetary conditions to cool inflation.
FALSE — Higher financing costs typically discourage investment spending.
FALSE — Cooling demand through tighter policy can lower inflation over time.

title: Vienna Mortgage Rate Shopping
context: Consider a Vienna household postponing a flat purchase after the central bank raises mortgage reference rates. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Higher saving returns after rate rises may shift some spending from consumption to deposits.
Postponing a flat purchase reduces current quantity demanded for housing credit.
Central bank rate rises aim to accelerate spending that contributes to inflation.
If many households delay purchases, equilibrium home prices rise because fewer buyers compete.
Higher mortgage reference rates reduce monthly borrowing costs for a given loan amount.

TRUE — Delayed buying lowers loan demand at present rates.
FALSE — Rate increases cool spending to fight inflation.
FALSE — Reduced demand typically eases upward price pressure.
FALSE — Higher rates increase loan costs, not reduce them.

title: Demand Increase at Equilibrium
context: Analyze how a rightward demand shift raises equilibrium price and quantity when supply is upward sloping. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Graphically, a demand shift right moves equilibrium up along an upward-sloping supply curve.
Producers respond to higher equilibrium price by reducing quantity supplied along the supply curve.
More buyers entering a market moves buyers along the demand curve without shifting it.
A rightward demand shift with unchanged supply lowers both equilibrium price and quantity.
After demand increases, quantity demanded stays below quantity supplied permanently.

FALSE — Higher prices incentivise greater quantity supplied along supply.
FALSE — More participants shift demand; own-price changes move along the curve.
FALSE — Demand increases with stable supply tend to raise price and quantity.
FALSE — New equilibrium restores equality between quantity demanded and supplied.

title: Supply Decrease at Equilibrium
context: Review how a leftward supply shift raises equilibrium price and lowers equilibrium quantity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: At the new equilibrium after supply falls, quantity demanded equals the reduced quantity supplied.
Buyers facing higher prices reduce quantity demanded along the demand curve after supply falls.
A leftward supply shift with unchanged demand typically raises equilibrium price and lowers quantity.
Production disruptions can shift supply leftward even when buyer preferences stay constant.
Graphically, a supply shift left moves equilibrium up along a downward-sloping demand curve.

TRUE — Price rise reduces quantity demanded along downward-sloping demand.
TRUE — Reduced supply at each price raises price and cuts quantity traded.
TRUE — Supply shifters change seller offerings independent of demand.
TRUE — New intersection lies up and to the left along demand.

title: Population Growth and Market Demand
context: Analyze how population changes shift market demand for goods and services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Markets adjust through price when population growth increases quantity demanded at old prices.
Population growth in a city can shift demand rightward for public transport services.
Immigration increasing local consumers can raise equilibrium apartment rents if housing supply is slow.
Demographic changes move buyers along the demand curve without shifting it.
A shrinking town population shifts demand rightward because remaining residents spend more.

TRUE — More residents increase quantity demanded at each price.
TRUE — Demand shift with limited short-run supply raises equilibrium price.
FALSE — Population is a non-price shifter that shifts the demand curve.
FALSE — Population decline typically reduces demand, not increases it automatically.

title: Taxes on Producers and Supply
context: Review how taxes levied on sellers can shift supply leftward. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A per-unit tax on producers raises effective production cost and can shift supply leftward.
The statutory incidence on producers can reduce market quantity below the prior equilibrium.
After a producer tax, sellers require lower prices to supply the same quantity as before.
Equilibrium price paid by buyers falls when producer taxes reduce quantity supplied.
Producer taxes move sellers along the supply curve without shifting it.

TRUE — Leftward supply shift lowers equilibrium quantity traded.
FALSE — Higher costs require higher prices to maintain the same quantity supplied.
FALSE — Lower supply with stable demand typically raises equilibrium price.
FALSE — Cost-changing taxes shift supply; own-price moves along the curve.

title: Subsidies to Producers and Supply
context: Analyze how payments to producers can shift supply rightward. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Subsidised farmers may supply more output at each market price after receiving per-unit payments.
Rightward supply shifts from subsidies raise equilibrium price if demand stays unchanged.
Subsidies differ from price ceilings because both cap buyer prices identically.
Taxpayer-funded subsidies reduce quantity supplied at each price by confusing producers.
Production subsidies lowering effective costs shift demand leftward for the subsidised good.

FALSE — More supply at unchanged demand tends to lower equilibrium price.
FALSE — Subsidies affect supply-side costs; ceilings limit legal prices.
FALSE — Improved margins from subsidies typically expand supply.
FALSE — Producer subsidies affect supply costs, not buyer demand directly.

title: Weather Shocks and Agricultural Supply
context: Review how adverse weather can shift agricultural supply leftward. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Drought reducing crop yields shifts supply leftward for affected harvests at each price.
Importers may partially offset domestic supply shifts by increasing quantity supplied from abroad.
Short-run food markets may show sharp price spikes after sudden supply leftward shifts.
Frost damaging orchards can raise equilibrium fruit prices if demand remains largely unchanged.
Weather shocks are demand-side events identical to changes in consumer tastes.

TRUE — External supply can shift total market supply rightward.
TRUE — Rapid supply cuts with sticky demand raise equilibrium price quickly.
TRUE — Leftward supply with stable demand raises equilibrium price.
FALSE — Weather affects supply conditions; tastes are demand shifters.

title: Consumer Expectations and Demand
context: Analyze how expectations about future prices or income shift current demand. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: If buyers expect prices to fall next month, current quantity demanded may decrease today.
Expectations of higher future petrol prices can shift current demand rightward as drivers stock up.
Expected future income growth may shift current demand rightward for durable goods like appliances.
Expectations about future conditions move buyers along the demand curve only.
Panic buying before announced rationing reflects a leftward demand shift at unchanged official prices.

TRUE — Anticipating future price rises increases current quantity demanded.
TRUE — Anticipated higher income raises willingness to buy now.
FALSE — Expectations shift demand; own-price changes move along the curve.
FALSE — Panic buying increases current demand before prices change.

title: Labour Market Wage Adjustment
context: Review how wages coordinate quantity supplied and demanded of labour like prices in goods markets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Labour market equilibrium occurs where quantity supplied of labour equals quantity demanded.
Competition among employers for scarce workers can bid wages up toward labour market equilibrium.
Higher wages typically reduce quantity supplied of labour as workers reject paid work.
Skill shortages in tech hiring resemble goods surpluses with downward wage pressure.
Employers hire more workers when wages rise above the value of marginal output at the margin.

TRUE — Employer bidding raises wages when quantity demanded exceeds supplied.
FALSE — Higher wages generally increase labour quantity supplied, ceteris paribus.
FALSE — Labour shortage implies excess demand and upward wage pressure.
FALSE — Higher wages raise labour costs and reduce quantity demanded.

title: Global Supply Chain Disruption
context: Analyze how international supply disruptions shift domestic market supply. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Domestic equilibrium price may rise when import supply falls while demand stays constant.
Global markets isolate domestic equilibrium from supply shocks abroad completely.
Firms may seek alternate suppliers over time, shifting demand leftward permanently.
Port closures delaying imports shift demand rightward for components used in domestic assembly.
Shortages of imported parts increase quantity supplied of finished goods domestically.

FALSE — Trade links domestic markets to foreign supply disruptions.
FALSE — Alternate suppliers affect supply recovery, not demand destruction.
FALSE — Import delays affect supply availability, not buyer demand directly.
FALSE — Missing inputs reduce feasible output and supply of finished goods.

title: Integrated Market Mechanisms Review
context: Review how demand, supply, equilibrium, and policy tools interact in competitive markets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Understanding markets requires separating movement along curves from shifts caused by other factors.
Inflation linked to excessive money growth may be addressed by tighter policy raising interest rates.
Price ceilings below equilibrium create shortage; price floors above equilibrium create surplus.
Demand shifters include income, tastes, and substitute prices; supply shifters include costs and technology.
Surplus and shortage signals guide competitive markets toward equilibrium through price adjustment.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Own-price changes differ from shifters on demand and supply sides.
TRUE — Monetary tightening cools spending that outpaces output.
TRUE — Binding caps and minimums produce predictable imbalances.
TRUE — Non-price determinants shift curves on each side of the market.
TRUE — Price changes coordinate divergent buyer and seller plans.

title: Capstone Scenarios in Market Analysis
context: Review applied combinations of demand shifts, supply shifts, and inflation policy in everyday economic settings. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Raising interest rates to fight inflation may slow housing demand by increasing mortgage costs.
